## Problem

Give an example of a Hilbert space which is not separable.

## Solution

Consider the Hilbert space

$$
\ell^2(\mathbb R)
=
\left\{
x=(x_i)_{i\in\mathbb R}:
\sum_{i\in\mathbb R}|x_i|^2<\infty
\right\},
$$

equipped with the inner product

$$
\langle x,y\rangle
=
\sum_{i\in\mathbb R}x_i\overline{y_i}.
$$

It is a standard fact that $\ell^2(\mathbb R)$ is a Hilbert space. We show that it is not separable.

For each $i\in\mathbb R$, define $e_i\in\ell^2(\mathbb R)$ by

$$
e_i(j)=\delta_{ij}.
$$

Then

$$
\{e_i:i\in\mathbb R\}
$$

is an uncountable orthonormal family. In particular, for any $i\neq j$,

$$
\|e_i-e_j\|=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Suppose, for contradiction, that $\ell^2(\mathbb R)$ is separable. Then there exists a countable dense subset $D\subset\ell^2(\mathbb R)$.

For each $i\in\mathbb R$, by the density of $D$, choose $d_i\in D$ such that

$$
\|e_i-d_i\|<\frac12.
$$

We claim that the points $d_i$ are all distinct. Indeed, if $d_i=d_j=d$ for some $i\neq j$, then by the triangle inequality,

$$
\|e_i-e_j\|
\le
\|e_i-d\|+\|d-e_j\|
<1,
$$

which contradicts

$$
\|e_i-e_j\|=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore the map

$$
i\longmapsto d_i
$$

is injective from $\mathbb R$ into $D$. Hence

$$
\operatorname{card}(D)
\ge
\operatorname{card}(\mathbb R),
$$

so $D$ is uncountable, contradicting our assumption.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{\ell^2(\mathbb R)\text{ is a nonseparable Hilbert space}.}
$$
